8:["$","$L13",null,{"data":{"chapterId":23,"verseId":2,"chapterTitle":"Examination of Error","totalVerses":25,"verseData":{"id":"v23_2","number":2,"title":"Afflictions Lack Inherent Existence Because Their Basis Does","sanskrit":{"text":"","transliteration":"","translation":"Since whatever depends on the pleasant and the unpleasant does not exist through an essence, the defilements do not really exist."},"philosophy":{"insight":"The EMPTINESS argument: afflictions depend on pleasant/unpleasant evaluations. These evaluations lack inherent essence (they're subjective and relative). Therefore: afflictions lack inherent existence too. Dependent on what's empty → itself empty.","madhyamaka":"Śubha aśubha āśritya yat tat svabhāvena na vidyate (what depends on pleasant/unpleasant doesn't exist through essence). Kleśāḥ na vidyante tattvataḥ (afflictions don't really exist). The chain: empty basis → empty dependent.","quantum":"If a quantum property depends on a measurement that itself has no absolute reference frame, the property has no absolute value. Relative measurement → relative property. Relative evaluation → relative affliction.","bridge":"Both: properties dependent on relative frameworks have no absolute value. QM: no absolute measurement frame → no absolute property. V.2: no absolute pleasant/unpleasant → no absolute affliction.","accessible":"\"Expensive\" depends on your income — a $100 meal is cheap for a millionaire, expensive for a student. Since \"expensive\" has no inherent essence, the emotion it triggers (desire or aversion) also lacks inherent essence.","twoTruths":"Conventionally: afflictions arise and cause real suffering. Ultimately: they lack inherent existence because their basis (pleasant/unpleasant) lacks inherent existence.","commonMisconception":"NOT saying emotions aren't real. They're CONVENTIONALLY real and cause real suffering. But they lack INHERENT existence — they're not fixed, permanent features of reality."},"quantumResonance":{"concept":"No Absolute Reference Frame → No Absolute Properties","score":55,"strength":"Medium","explanation":"QM: no absolute measurement frame → no absolute property values. V.2: no inherent pleasant/unpleasant → no inherent afflictions. Both: relative bases yield relative (non-absolute) dependents.","caveat":"Reference frames are physics. V.2 is about evaluative bases. The parallel is about the non-absolute nature of framework-dependent properties."},"animation":{"visualBridge":"A chain: \"Pleasant/Unpleasant\" (glowing) → \"Afflictions\" (derived glow). When the basis fades (shown as empty), the afflictions fade too. Caption: \"Empty basis → empty afflictions.\"","educationalGoal":"Afflictions inherit emptiness from their basis. Empty evaluations → empty emotions."},"deeperDive":[{"q":"Why are pleasant/unpleasant evaluations empty?","a":"They're SUBJECTIVE and RELATIVE — the same object is pleasant to one person and unpleasant to another. There's no inherent \"pleasantness\" in the object. The evaluation depends on the subject.","realLifeExample":"Spicy food: pleasant to some, unpleasant to others. The spiciness is objective; the evaluation is subjective. No inherent pleasantness."},{"q":"How does empty basis imply empty dependent?","a":"If X depends on Y, and Y lacks inherent existence, then X can't have inherent existence either. Inherent existence would require an inherent basis. Empty basis → empty dependent. Like a reflection depending on a mirror — no mirror, no reflection.","realLifeExample":"A shadow depends on an object. If the object is a hologram (empty of substance), the shadow is equally insubstantial."},{"q":"Does this mean afflictions don't cause suffering?","a":"No — they CONVENTIONALLY cause suffering. But understanding their emptiness weakens their grip. An affliction seen as empty has less power than one seen as inherently real. Emptiness doesn't eliminate convention — it reveals its nature.","realLifeExample":"Knowing a nightmare is \"just a dream\" doesn't make it disappear instantly, but it reduces its power. Seeing afflictions as empty has the same effect."},{"q":"How does this build on v.1?","a":"V.1: afflictions arise from conceptual evaluation. V.2: since the evaluation is empty, the afflictions are empty. V.1 = dependent origination. V.2 = therefore empty.","realLifeExample":"V.1: your mood depends on your interpretation. V.2: since interpretations are relative (not inherent), moods are also relative. Chain of emptiness."},{"q":"What is the significance for practice?","a":"If afflictions are empty (not inherently real), they can be TRANSFORMED through understanding. This is the philosophical basis for meditation, therapy, and the Buddhist path. Inherent afflictions would be untreatable; empty afflictions are workable.","realLifeExample":"A knot that's \"inherently tied\" could never be untied. A conventionally tied knot CAN be untied. Emptiness = workability."},{"q":"How does this relate to the quantum parallel?","a":"In QM, a property measured relative to one frame may differ from another frame. There's no absolute value. Similarly, an evaluation of \"pleasant\" is relative to the evaluator. No absolute pleasant → no absolute desire.","deeper":"V.2 establishes the key inference: dependent on empty → itself empty. This principle is used throughout Madhyamaka: whatever depends on something that lacks inherent existence itself lacks inherent existence. Applied to afflictions: they depend on empty evaluations, therefore they're empty. This is both a theoretical insight and a practical tool — seeing the empty chain from evaluation to affliction weakens the affliction's apparent solidity."}],"quiz":{"beginner":{"question":"Why do afflictions lack inherent existence?","options":["A) They're inherent","B) They depend on pleasant/unpleasant evaluations, which are subjective and relative (empty). The chain of emptiness."},"intermediate":{"question":"Does emptiness of afflictions mean they don't cause suffering?","options":["A) Yes","B) No — they CONVENTIONALLY cause suffering. But seeing their emptiness weakens their grip. Empty ≠ non-existent; empty = not inherently fixed.","C) Sometimes","D) Only for advanced practitioners"],"correct":"B","explanation":"Conventional suffering continues.
